rationale: B wins because it finds three real routes without selling the facts a costume. Its pricing angle, "Why Mindbody isn't charging extra for AI," uses a supplied fact and turns it into a reporter-shaped business question; A's ClassPass angle, "now its AI sits on top of both," walks past the evidence and asks proof to clean up after the headline. A is smart, but B is safer strategic material because its caveats are built into the angle, not bolted on after the overclaim.
gaps_in_A: "now its AI sits on top of both" is not in the update. Mindbody owns ClassPass, but nothing says this assistant uses ClassPass data, inventory, or demand.
"using aggregated booking data across the network" invents scope. The update says booking data, not cross-network aggregation.
"software decides the schedule" overstates the product. The fact is that it suggests optimal class times; adoption by studios is still unproven.
"cut studio no-show rates 22% by texting the waitlist" compresses a company-reported pilot into causation. It needs methodology before that headline can stand up.
gaps_in_B: It leaves the supplied ClassPass ownership fact mostly in the penalty box. The hallucinated ClassPass-user angle deserved refusal, but a narrower platform-power question could have been kept.
"salon trade outlet" stretches the stakeholder. The launch is for boutique fitness and wellness studios; salons are scale context, not the clean class-cancellation protagonist.
"Why Mindbody isn't charging extra for AI" is directionally fair, but "bundled into existing software tiers" is the safer wording until pricing mechanics are confirmed.
